nameStory: Sharp-leaved Blindia gets its name from its distinctly pointed, needle-like leaves that feel sharp to the touch. The genus name 'Blindia' honors Irish botanist Thomas Blind, though ironically, you'll need sharp eyes and good magnification to spot this tiny moss in the field!
description: Sharp-leaved Blindia is a tiny cushion-forming moss that creates small, dense mounds on rocks and soil. Individual plants are barely noticeable, growing only a few millimeters tall, but they often cluster together to form compact cushions about the size of a quarter. This diminutive moss has a dark green to blackish-green color when moist, turning brownish when dry. It's one of New England's smaller mosses, easily overlooked without careful observation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, sharp-pointed leaves that feel prickly when rubbed gently with your finger. They're tightly packed and stand somewhat erect, giving the plant a spiky texture even when moist.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms small, tight cushions or mats that feel firm and springy when pressed. Individual cushions are usually smaller than a coin but may merge with neighboring patches.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark green to nearly black when wet, shifting to brownish-green or rusty brown when dry. The color change is quite dramatic and happens quickly as moisture levels change.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on exposed rock surfaces, especially granite and other acidic rocks. Prefers spots that get some moisture but aren't constantly wet.

idTips.label: Sporophytes
idTips.description: Tiny capsules on short stalks appear occasionally, looking like miniature brown or reddish pins sticking up from the cushions. Most easily seen in late spring to early summer.

habitat: Sharp-leaved Blindia grows on exposed rock surfaces, particularly granite outcrops, stone walls, and rocky ledges throughout New England's mountains and hills. It prefers acidic rocks in areas that receive some moisture from rain or mist but aren't constantly soggy. You'll often find it in partial shade on north-facing rock faces or in the crevices of old stone walls.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green as spring rains arrive, and sporophytes (if present) begin developing. This is often the best time to spot the tiny reproductive structures.
seasonality.summer: May appear brownish and dormant during dry spells but quickly greens up after summer rains. Mature sporophytes are most visible in early summer.
seasonality.fall: Stays active through fall rains, returning to its deep green color. Often more noticeable as other vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Remains present but may be hard to spot under snow. During winter thaws, it can photosynthesize and appears surprisingly green against gray rocks.

funFact: This tiny moss can lose up to 95% of its water content and appear completely dead, then spring back to life within minutes of getting wet—a survival trick that lets it thrive on exposed rocks where other plants would quickly perish!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, dark cushion mosses on rocks, especially Grimmia species. Sharp-leaved Blindia's leaves are more needle-like and prickly to the touch, while Grimmia mosses tend to have softer, more rounded leaf tips. Remember: if it feels genuinely sharp and prickly, think Blindia.
contextualKnowledge: Sharp-leaved Blindia is extremely rare in New England, with only a single confirmed observation in the region. This makes any sighting potentially significant for botanical records, so careful documentation with photos and location data is especially valuable if you think you've found it.
compareHints: With no other Blindia species in New England, compare it to similar small rock mosses in the Grimmia genus. Blindia's leaves are more sharply pointed and the overall plant typically forms tighter, more compact cushions. The prickly texture when touched is distinctly different from the softer feel of most Grimmia species, even when both are dry.
